video_caption: The video begins with a close-up on a white plastic container with a blue lid, labeled "J.T. Baker" and containing "Sodium Chloride, Crystal" (Chlorure de Sodium), with chemical formula NaCl, a formula weight of 58.44, and a quantity of "2.5 kg." The label specifies it as "'BAKER ANALYZED' A.C.S. Reagent" with lot number G04584 and CAS No: 7647-14-5. The camera then slowly zooms out to reveal a broader view of a laboratory setup on a dark countertop. The container is positioned next to a clear graduated cylinder, a small beaker resting on a white hot plate, a small white dish filled with white powder, and a digital scale displaying a reading of 0.000 g. A power cord is plugged into a wall outlet in the background, next to a silver piece of equipment. The scene then transitions to a close-up of a clear microscope slide, held by a hand wearing a purple glove. On the surface of the slide, white crystalline structures, including distinct square-shaped formations, are visible against a dark background, appearing to be growing or drying.

The video segment opens with a person wearing purple gloves using a pipette to drop a clear liquid onto a glass slide placed inside a petri dish on a dark countertop. This person, now also wearing a white lab coat and a face mask, is then shown opening a white scientific oven/incubator, branded "Thermo Scientific" with a digital display showing "80," and placing something small inside on a rack, indicating a drying or heating process. The scene transitions to a "BRUKER D8 FOCUS Xtop" X-ray diffractometer, a large scientific machine with a clear top enclosure revealing its internal mechanisms, and a yellow "CAUTION HIGH INTENSITY X-RAY BEAM" sticker, implying the next step involves X-ray diffraction analysis. Following this, the person in purple gloves is seen grinding a white powdery substance in a white mortar with a pestle. The video then displays a laboratory setup on a dark surface, featuring a hot plate stirrer with a beaker, a graduated cylinder, a large container of "Baker Sodium Chloride, Crystal," a small plastic weigh boat with white powder, and a digital scale, suggesting preparation for an experiment. The camera zooms in on the white powder in the weigh boat, and then on the label of the "Baker Sodium Chloride, Crystal" container, which reads: "2.5 kg Baker Sodium Chloride, Crystal Chlorure de Sodium 'BAKER ANALYZED' A.C.S. Reagent NaCl ACTUAL ANALYSIS, LOT G04584 FW 58.44 MADE IN USA." (This text identifies the chemical as 2.5 kg of Baker-analyzed sodium chloride crystals, chemical formula NaCl, with a specific lot number and formula weight, produced in the USA). An overlay text "Prepare a 50 mL solution of 1 M NaCl" appears on screen, indicating the objective of preparing a 50 milliliter solution of 1 molar sodium chloride.

The segment displays a close-up of a white plastic container labeled "Baker" on the left side, containing "Sodium Chloride, Crystal" (Chlorure de Sodium). The label also states "2.5 kg," "'BAKER ANALYZED' A.C.S. Reagent," "NaCl," "ACTUAL ANALYSIS, LOT G04584," "CAS NO: 7647-14-5," and "MADE IN USA." A yellow box highlights the "FW 58.44" (Formula Weight) on the container. Overlay text at the top left corner reads "Prepare a 50 mL solution of 1 M NaCl," while text below it specifies "Mw = 58.44 g/mol," further emphasizing the molecular weight of sodium chloride.

A person wearing a lab coat and purple gloves first places a plastic weigh boat onto an electronic balance, tares the scale from "4.16" to "0.00", and then uses a metal spatula to carefully add 2.92 grams of white powdered sodium chloride from another weigh boat onto the scale. Next, the person measures out 50 mL of deionized water from a squeeze bottle, labeled "DEIONIZED WATER" with a hazard diamond, into a graduated cylinder marked "CHEMISTA TM 20024 20 °C 50 ml," ensuring the meniscus aligns with the 50 mL line. This water is then poured into a "Fisherbrand 150ml" glass beaker containing a PTFE-coated magnetic stir rod. The beaker is placed on a VWR-branded stir plate, and the stirring function is activated, creating a vortex in the water. The weighed sodium chloride is then added to the stirred water, and the solution is allowed to mix until the salt completely dissolves, indicated by a clear liquid. Finally, a clean glass slide is placed inside a clear petri dish, and the person uses a transfer pipette to carefully deposit a droplet of the newly prepared sodium chloride solution onto the center of the glass slide.

The video segment opens with a close-up shot of a clear glass petri dish containing a small, black rectangular substrate resting on its bottom. A person wearing a purple glove uses a clear plastic dropper to dispense a clear liquid onto the center of the black substrate, forming a distinct, spherical droplet. The scene then transitions to a wider shot of a laboratory environment, featuring a white "Thermo Scientific" incubator with a blue control panel displaying the number "80" (likely indicating 80 degrees Celsius) on its front. A person, wearing a white lab coat, purple gloves, and a white face mask, opens the incubator door, revealing metal racks inside, and carefully places a small, flat object onto one of the racks before closing the door. Various charts and laboratory equipment are visible in the background.

In a laboratory setting, a person wearing a white lab coat and purple gloves uses a spatula to transfer white, crystalline powder from a small plastic container into a white ceramic mortar. The ceramic pestle rests beside the mortar on a dark countertop. After transferring a sufficient amount of powder, the person picks up the pestle and begins to grind the white substance within the mortar, holding the mortar steady with their non-dominant hand. The video provides a close-up of the grinding action, showing the powder being crushed into a finer consistency. On the black surface of the lab bench, next to the mortar, a clear circular petri dish lid and a rectangular microscope slide are visible. The rhythmic sound of grinding is audible as the process continues, aiming to reduce the sodium chloride crystals into a fine powder for X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis.

A person wearing purple gloves is seen in a lab setting, first using a pestle to stir white powder in a white ceramic mortar bowl. They then use a small metal spatula to carefully transfer a small amount of this white powder into a clear circular sample holder, gently spreading it around to ensure the top surface is flush with the holder's edge. This process is repeated to add more powder, filling the sample holder. Finally, the person picks up a rectangular glass slide and uses its edge to meticulously level the surface of the powder in the sample holder, moving the slide back and forth with light pressure to achieve a smooth and even finish before removing it.

The video opens with a hand wearing a purple glove placing a clear, circular disc with a white powdery center onto a dark surface, next to a small, white ceramic bowl containing a white, granular substance. The scene then transitions to a close-up of a clear glass slide where small, square-shaped white crystals begin to appear and grow, forming distinct clusters in one corner over a short time. Finally, the video shows a different clear glass slide being held by the purple-gloved hand, displaying a larger, irregular, and textured mass of white crystalline material, also composed of numerous small, square crystals that have grown together.

The video segment opens with a shot of a Bruker D8 FOCUS X-ray Diffractometer (XRD) machine, a large grey scientific instrument with a glass enclosure on top revealing complex internal components, and a yellow "CAUTION X-RAY RADIATION" sign on its front. A person wearing purple gloves then holds a small rectangular glass slide with a shimmering, irregularly shaped sample on it. This person proceeds to place the glass slide onto a metal sample holder, pressing it gently into a central blue polymer clay substance to secure it. They carefully manipulate the slide, lifting and re-positioning it to ensure the top surface of the sample aligns perfectly with the top plane of the sample holder. After achieving the desired alignment, the prepared sample holder is shown resting on a white surface, with another blank glass slide nearby. The scene then transitions to the interior of the XRD machine, where the sample holder with the prepared sample is mounted and ready for analysis. Overlaid on this shot is a graph displaying data, with the text "NaCl (100) crystal orientation" visible, illustrating the type of measurement or result from the XRD.

The video segment opens with two data graphs prominently displayed against a blurred background of laboratory equipment, specifically an X-ray diffractometer with a large circular component. The graph on the left, labeled "NaCl powder" in blue, shows an X-ray diffraction pattern with several sharp peaks, indicating random orientation of crystallites. The graph on the right, labeled "NaCl crystal on glass" in orange, exhibits a diffraction pattern with a few very strong, dominant peaks, suggesting a preferred orientation of crystals. Both graphs share the same axes: "Intensity (a.u.)" on the Y-axis and "2θ / Cu-Kα / °" on the X-axis. A male voice discusses that this data will be provided for students to analyze, asking what conclusions can be drawn about the preferred orientation of crystal growth from evaporating salt solution on glass slides. As the voice concludes, the screen darkens, and production credits appear in white and gold text, reading: "© 2020 Zachary Neale. This video is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0", "Production Zachary Neale Tatyana Galenko", "Location University of Washington, Seattle Mueller and Roberts Hall", and "Music idling around by Diamond Ace | https://soundcloud.com/diamond-ace-music Music promoted by https://www.free-stock-music.com". The lab background remains faintly visible beneath the text.
